==Problem==
The one-way routes connecting towns <imath>A,M,C,X,Y,</imath> and <imath>Z</imath> are shown in the figure below(not drawn to scale).The distances in kilometers along each route are marked. Traveling along these routes, what is the shortest distance from A to Z in kilometers?

<asy>
/* AMC8 P14 2024, by NUMANA: BUI VAN HIEU */
import graph;
unitsize(2cm);
real r=0.25;
// Define the nodes and their positions
pair[] nodes = { (0,0), (2,0), (1,1), (3,1), (4,0), (6,0) };
string[] labels = { "A", "M", "X", "Y", "C", "Z" };

// Draw the nodes as circles with labels
for(int i = 0; i < nodes.length; ++i) {
    draw(circle(nodes[i], r));
    label("$" + labels[i] + "$", nodes[i]);
}
// Define the edges with their node indices and labels
int[][] edges = { {0, 1}, {0, 2}, {2, 1}, {2, 3}, {1, 3}, {1, 4}, {3, 4}, {4, 5}, {3, 5} };
string[] edgeLabels = { "8", "5", "2", "10", "6", "14", "5", "10", "17" };
pair[] edgeLabelsPos = { S, SE, SW, S, SE, S, SW, S, NE};
// Draw the edges with labels
for (int i = 0; i < edges.length; ++i) {
    pair start = nodes[edges[i][0]];
    pair end = nodes[edges[i][1]];
    draw(start + r*dir(end-start) -- end-r*dir(end-start), Arrow);
    label("$" + edgeLabels[i] + "$", midpoint(start -- end),  edgeLabelsPos[i]);
}
// Draw the curved edge with label
draw(nodes[1]+r * dir(-45)..controls (3, -0.75) and (5, -0.75)..nodes[5]+r * dir(-135), Arrow);
label("$25$", midpoint(nodes[1]..controls (3, -0.75) and (5, -0.75)..nodes[5]), 2S);
</asy>

<imath>\textbf{(A)}\ 28 \qquad \textbf{(B)}\ 29 \qquad \textbf{(C)}\ 30 \qquad \textbf{(D)}\ 31 \qquad \textbf{(E)}\ 32</imath>

==Solution 1==

We can simply see that path <imath>A \rightarrow X \rightarrow M \rightarrow Y \rightarrow C \rightarrow Z</imath> will give us the smallest value. Adding, <imath>5+2+6+5+10 = \boxed{28}</imath>. This is nice as it’s also the smallest value, solidifying our answer.

You can also simply brute-force it or sort of think ahead - for example, getting from A to M can be done <imath>2</imath> ways; <imath>A \rightarrow X \rightarrow M</imath> (<imath>5+2</imath>) or <imath>A \rightarrow M (8)</imath>, so you should take the shorter route (<imath>5+2</imath>). Another example is M to C, two ways - one is <imath>6+5</imath> and the other is <imath>14</imath>. Take the shorter route. After this, you need to consider a few more times - consider if <imath>5+10</imath> (<imath>Y \rightarrow C \rightarrow Z</imath>) is greater than <imath>17 (Y \rightarrow Z</imath>), which it is not, and consider if <imath>25 (M \rightarrow Z</imath>) is greater than <imath>14+10</imath> (<imath>M \rightarrow C \rightarrow Z</imath>) or <imath>6+5+10</imath> (<imath>M \rightarrow Y \rightarrow C \rightarrow Z</imath>) which it is not. TLDR: <imath>5+2+6+5+10 = \boxed{28}</imath>. [Note: This is probably just the thinking behind the solution.] {Double-note: As MaxyMoosy said, since this answer is the smallest one, it has to be the right answer.}

==Solution 2 (Advanced)==
We can execute [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dijkstra%27s_algorithm Dijkstra's algorithm] by hand to find the shortest path from <imath>A</imath> to every other town, including <imath>Z</imath>. This effectively proves that, assuming we execute the algorithm correctly, that we will have found the shortest distance. The distance estimates for each step of the algorithm (from <imath>A</imath> to each node) are shown below:

<cmath>\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline
\text{Current node} & A & M & C & X & Y & Z \\ \hline
A & 0 & 8 & \infty & 5 & \infty & \infty \\
X & 0 & 7 & \infty & 5 & 15 & \infty \\
M & 0 & 7 & 21 & 5 & 13 & 32 \\
Y & 0 & 7 & 18 & 5 & 13 & 30 \\
C & 0 & 7 & 18 & 5 & 13 & 28 \\
Z & 0 & 7 & 18 & 5 & 13 & \textbf{28} \\ \hline
\end{array}</cmath>
The steps are as follows: starting with the initial node <imath>A</imath>, set <imath>d(A)=0</imath> and <imath>d(v)=\infty</imath> for all <imath>v \in \{M,C,X,Y,Z\}</imath> where <imath>d(v)</imath> indicates the distance from <imath>A</imath> to <imath>v</imath>. Consider the outgoing edges <imath>(A,X)</imath> and <imath>(A,M)</imath> and update the distance estimates <imath>d(X)=5</imath> and <imath>d(M)=8</imath>, completing the first row of the table.

The node <imath>X</imath> is the unvisited node with the lowest distance estimate, so we will consider <imath>X</imath> and its outgoing edges <imath>(X,Y)</imath> and <imath>(X,M)</imath>. The distance estimate <imath>d(Y)</imath> equals <imath>d(X)+10=15</imath>, and the distance estimate <imath>d(M)</imath> updates to <imath>d(X)+2=7</imath>, because <imath>7 < 8</imath>. This completes the second row of the table. Repeating this process for each unvisited node (in order of its distance estimate) yields the correct distance <imath>d(Z) = \boxed{\textbf{(A) } 28}</imath> once the algorithm is complete.

~scrabbler94


==Solution 3 (Variant of Solution 1)==

From <imath>A</imath>, we want to find the shortest route to <imath>Z</imath>, so we want to try to find the shortest path through each node (not necessarily all of them). We should follow the arrows, since all of them lead to <imath>Z</imath>. From <imath>A</imath>, there are <imath>2</imath> paths we can take, to <imath>M</imath> <imath>(8)</imath>, or to <imath>X</imath> <imath>(5)</imath>. We travel to <imath>X</imath>, since <imath>5 < 8</imath>. From <imath>X</imath>, we go to <imath>M</imath> <imath>(2 < 10)</imath>, we go to <imath>Y</imath> <imath>6 < 14 < 25</imath>, we go to <imath>C</imath>, <imath>(5 < 17)</imath> and finally go to <imath>Z</imath>. Adding up gives <imath>5 + 2 + 6 + 5 + 10 = 28 = \boxed{\textbf{(A)}}</imath>.

~SpeedCuber7

==Solution 4 (On paper)==
We can cross off a few routes:
*AM can be crossed off because AXM is shorter
*XY can be crossed off because XMY is shorter
*YZ can be crossed off because YCZ is shorter
*MC can be crossed off because MYC is shorter
*MZ can be crossed off because MCZ is shorter
Finally, we are left with a single path AXMYCZ from A to Z which adding it up gives <imath>28 = \boxed{\textbf{(A)}}.</imath>
